items.object: Homogeneity in language model outputs
items.answer: Even for open-ended questions, the models are not as diverse as we would have expected, to the point that even when you ask multiple times with higher temperature, it may not be able to vary as much. items.object: Reasoning in small language models and alignment with pluralistic norms and values

items.question: What drives your interest in small language models as a way to democratize generative AI?
items.object: Small language models and democratizing generative AI
items.answer: The mission really is democratizing generative AI, so that it's not just companies who can purchase a lot of GPUs that are able to create LLMs, adopt LLMs, and serve LLMs, but also people like myself and colleagues who are academics. For example, we cannot buy as many GPUs. Is there something really meaningful and fun that we could do even with a smaller counterpart? At the end of the day, I believe that fundamentally it should be feasible. It's only that the world has invested so much more into exploring what happens when you scale things up so much. Whereas if we invested even a fraction of that investment, just a little bit more, I do think that we can unlock a lot more exciting capabilities out of small language models.

items.question: Why do you want to find more data-efficient ways of teaching intelligence to machines?
items.object: Data-efficient approaches to teaching machines intelligence
items.answer: Part of my research is also driven by the desire to find really better ways of teaching intelligence to machines. Currently it's just so data-centric. We can talk about that in more detail later in this podcast. But it's so data-dependent, and that's pretty much the only way we know how to teach AI about human knowledge and intelligence. In the future, I don't know whether we will find the solution or not, but as an academic I feel like we have to give it a try to find an entirely better solution to this that is so much more data-efficient and able to learn so much more with much less data.

items.question: How do you view the AI industry's concentration of effort on making models larger?
items.object: The AI industry's concentration on scaling models
items.answer:
There's definitely a snowball effect and then a ship-herding effect. You see other ships going where, and then you want to follow that because it's a safe choice, especially when raising funding is relatively—not as hard as it used to be for AI. Therefore that's guaranteed and proven ways of increasing intelligence. So why not?

In fact, I'm not against such effort. It's really interesting to see and watch how much intelligence scale can unlock. I appreciate that some people went crazy and found out the frontier of what happens with scale. Having said that, I do worry about everybody trying the same thing. I think it's very important that we try different ideas. Historically, whatever innovation happened with computers or phones, they're always very large at the beginning, and then over the course of time people figure out how to make it smaller yet more powerful. The same thing will definitely happen with generative AI as well. In fact, already there's a lot of research effort that makes models smaller but more powerful. And I think we can do so much more, so much better, if we put more mind and effort into it.

items.question: How do you think about the different approaches to making small language models more powerful?
items.object: Approaches to making small language models more powerful
items.answer:
There are multiple routes. At the beginning, people were trying to think about compressing larger models into smaller models by either quantizing them or pruning some neurons and stuff like this. So that's, in some sense, an optimization-based or a little bit more mechanical optimization-based approach to making larger models into smaller models. And it does require larger models in order to make smaller models. So there's that. Nothing wrong with that. It's nice to have that option, but it's not the only way.

In the short term, I think having new architectures, like some hybrid between state machines and conventional transformers, like Mamba Hybrid from Nvidia, for example, could be an alternative way of making small models more powerful. But there can be other ways, such as making data better, especially providing much more powerful data. This data usually has to be at the outer skirts of internet data, meaning the kind of data that the internet couldn't quite provide in order to teach the model to do certain kinds of reasoning better. If we have much higher quality data, usually small models learn so much faster. So that's another way.

items.question: What do you mean by better training data beyond what is available on the internet?
items.object: Better training data beyond internet data
items.answer:
Let me clarify what I meant by better data, because internet data is not so bad, at least in terms of quantity. When we look at the LLM pipeline, a pretrained model is never good enough, despite its scale. You have to do post-training on a fairly large amount of data that usually is different from the internet data. Supervised fine-tuning, as well as RL, requires the kind of data points that are either curated by humans just for the purpose of teaching AI. These are not things that you just downloaded from the internet, but maybe you pay someone to write those data points.

The more common practice these days is not even crowdsourcing your data, but rather hiring experts like lawyers, former international math olympiad winners. These are real experts, and then you have them write data for you. So a lot of expert data is being collected as well.

items.question: How do you think synthetic data generation can produce reasoning examples that are qualitatively better than internet data?
items.object: Synthetic data generation for reasoning
items.answer:
Even that is not enough for AI because AI is so data-dependent. More recently, people also do a lot of automatic synthetic data generation. If you do it in a more vanilla way, just ask LLMs to write some problems or solutions for you, then oftentimes it's not good enough, or it could just be repetition of the same thing. It does require a lot more effort in the way that you design the prompt and then have a pipeline of different models making the prompt better or making the solution better, revising the solution, taking lots of iterations. So it's not as simple as just asking ChatGPT to write data for you.

If we do it quite right, then it can lead to a new data point that didn't exist on the internet. It could be really high-quality data that is qualitatively different from what was on the internet. A prime example of this is hard math solutions. Internet data does have a lot of math, but it doesn't necessarily have solutions to a lot of hard math problems. So you have to come up with those solutions either by asking experts to write solutions for you or using LLMs in some ways in order to generate good solutions, even though they're not quite capable of doing it yet. But you could use reinforcement learning with verifiers that can explore a lot and see which solutions AI generated happen to be correct based on the verifier. Then you collect that data, which is implicitly used as good data during RL to amplify that model behavior. Sometimes people then use those data points in order to do imitation learning on top, iteratively.

items.object: Mode collapse in large language model generation
items.answer: Mode collapse is a real concern with LLM generation, because what we find in our paper is that even when you ask open-ended questions, like "Tell me a joke about time," or "Tell me something wise about time," or "Tell me a story about something," you would expect that, well, there's no one good answer. Therefore, language models should be able to generate a diverse set of solutions. Even when you ask, "Hey, give me a random number between zero and ten," it's not random.

items.question: Why are you concerned about the internet increasingly containing LLM-generated writing?
items.object: The internet as an artifact of human intelligence
items.answer: It's a bit of a concern to me because more and more people utilize LLMs in order to post things on the internet. I wonder what happens to our internet. The internet used to be the artifact of human intelligence. It really encapsulates the vastly different ways people write and think, and is a historical artifact of human intelligence. Now it's really becoming the artifact of LLMs mixed with some amount of human intelligence. What if it becomes more homogeneous and less reflective of the diverse spectrum of human thoughts? Now we're going to lose something valuable, is my concern.

items.question: How do you think research on homogeneous LLM output should extend beyond its effects on model training?
items.object: The effects of homogeneous LLM output and synthetic articles on human thinking
items.answer:
It's interesting that folks that use a variety of LLMs see this behavior a lot. You ask a fairly open-ended question across multiple LLMs and you get very similar responses.

In the context of training data, the question is often asked: How do we improve models if models are, quote unquote, smoking their own exhaust, or training on this synthetic data? The implication is that we accelerate further mode collapse. But what I found interesting about this paper is that, yes, there's that, but not only that: What is the impact on the reader, the ecosystem, the humans that are in this environment where this synthetic data is being posted as articles? Is it hive mind? Is it changing the way we're thinking?

The broader thought was, you're affiliated with HAI. That seems like the place to cross-interdisciplinarily study this. I'd be super interested in hearing more about that. Let me know if you hear any work in that regard.

items.question: How do you think AI research should be directed to benefit humanity?
items.object: Research priorities for AI that benefits humanity
items.answer:
I do think that LLMs doing really well on method data and method problems won't necessarily be the most beneficial one for humanity. That's one crude way of saying it, but that kind of encapsulates what I believe about the future of AI on humanity, which is that we really have to work on specific problems more explicitly. If we care about democracy, we need to work on designing AI that can make humans more democratic, understand each other through democratic process, and work with different opinions through democratic process, as opposed to building AI that really optimizes for people's attention and engagement with the feeds that could increase the tension among us, because profit incentives are not necessarily aligned with what humanity at large should aspire to achieve.

In order to get what we want, we cannot just leave it to a few tech companies doing their wonderful jobs. I'm sure they have a lot of members in their companies who have good intentions. But it could also be that, especially when there's profit competition and engagement competition, things could unroll in a way that is not as beneficial for humanity.

items.question: What does AI democratization mean to you?
items.object: AI democratization
items.answer: When I think about AI democratization, I really think about the way that I like to think about it: AI of humans, for humans, and by humans. If it's AI for humans, it should really be AI for all humans, not just some humans working for some companies in some countries. If we are not very careful with how we design AI, I think it could come to a point where it's not even AI for humans, but it's more like AI for AI, and even worse, humans for AI, humans working for AI, essentially. For that I think it's very important for nonprofit sectors to participate in designing the future of AI, not just the profit sectors.

items.question: How do you think about the challenge of making small language models better reasoners?
items.object: Improving reasoning in small language models
items.answer: I'm quite excited about making small language models better reasoners, especially because reasoning is such an important intelligence capability that any model in the future has to be good at. This is an interesting challenge because internet data doesn't really equip LLMs to reason well right away. They can reason to some degree, but they do require a lot more post-training in order to infuse better reasoning capabilities. My research has recently focused on how to make small models reason better. That requires both feeding in better data through a sequential fine-tuning phase, and that data has to be really high-quality and diverse, as well as other kinds of algorithmic approaches that can squeeze out better intelligence even from small language models that seemed kind of hopeless.

items.question: How do you use Prismatic Synthesis to make synthetic math training data from a smaller teacher model compete with data from a much larger teacher?
items.object: Prismatic Synthesis and diversity in synthetic training data
items.answer:
I think there's a huge future in synthetic data. I can give you one example of our recent work called Prismatic Synthesis. It's a synthetic data generation algorithm which is prismatic because it acts a little bit like a prism that can scatter the light to make it more diversified.

What we do is basically math problem synthesis—actually, it's more like math problem and solution synthesis—and we're doing this using a DeepSeek R1 32-billion-parameter model as the teacher model. Now, 32B parameters is medium size, a little bit bigger than medium size these days, but it's much worse than DeepSeek R1, the full model, the biggest model, which is a 671B parameter model. That's like 20 times bigger than the model that we choose to use as teacher model in this work. We primarily focus on making sequential fine-tuning data for hard math problems using this medium-scale teacher model, and our goal is to compete against the alternative, which is to use a much stronger teacher that's 20 times larger.

In general, that's a really difficult game to play. It's really hard to beat against a teacher that's 20 times larger because the performance gap is significant. How on earth do we close the gap? Algorithmic ways of filtering the data to ensure the diversity of the generated data. No matter how good your teacher is, as we demonstrated in our Artificial Hive Mind paper, they're all repetitive, they're all homogeneous. So you have to put a lot of effort into diversifying them.

The way that we diversify data is we look at the gradient vector of output given input using a proxy model, a small-scale proxy model. It's so small, it's only a 1.5-billion-parameter model. These output-input pairs are the synthetic data that we just synthesized using the DeepSeek R1 32-billion-parameter model.

It's an old-fashioned clustering mechanism that still works in this modern day. items.question: Why do you generate math problems synthetically rather than rely on problems from the internet?
items.object: Generating synthetic math problems
items.answer: It's just some hard math problem. They're all hard math that requires a very long solution. When we autogenerate all the solutions, we have no idea whether the answer is correct or not, right? In our case, it's fully synthetic, even for the problems—many other synthetic data approaches rely on problems that exist on the internet, so that you only solve legitimate problems. But in our case, we generate the problems as well because we really wanted to explore a diverse scope of the math reasoning domain.

items.question: How do you assess answer consistency as a way to control synthetic math data quality without human validation?
items.object: Answer consistency as a filter for synthetic math data
items.answer: These solutions generated for fake problems may or may not be correct. So what we do is ask the model to solve the same problem multiple times and then check whether the final answer is identical each time. If not, then we worry that the quality might be bad. It's a very crude way of filtering data, but it worked well enough for our case, and I think this is a powerful method to use for controlling the quality of synthetic data without human validation.

items.question: Why do you change the examples in your prompts across iterations of synthetic math problem generation?
items.object: Varying prompt examples across iterations of synthetic math problem generation
items.answer: For prompting, we show some examples: "Generate math problems of this kind." What we change through these multiple iterations of overgeneration and filtering is the examples that we show in the prompt. The examples come from the previous iterations, in the hope that the models may feel more inspired when provided with newer, more different examples in the context.

items.question: What do you see as the guiding principle behind generating synthetic training data in stages to maintain diversity?
items.object: Diversity-focused synthetic training-data generation
items.answer: Depending on how you view it, it's a simple idea and a simple method, which is the big benefit of this method. The principle here is that you really want to make data that's qualitatively different from the internet data that's easy to generate. You really need to go to these relatively less explored regions. Of course, you need to make sure that the quality is reasonably good there as well, but it's really a diversity that we are trying to quantitatively enhance in the data set production.

items.question: Why do you see making out-of-distribution cases in-distribution as central to improving today's generative AI models?
items.object: Making out-of-distribution cases in-distribution through training
items.answer:
I think that alone can really go quite far. If you really cover diverse ground, your model can perform so much better, because at the end of the day current LLMs, no matter how amazing they are, are only as good as the data that they were trained on. You have to show similar examples. The more similar examples, the better for whatever the model may have to deal with during test time. The way that I like to put it is that whatever is out of distribution, just make it in-distribution. Make sure that you make all the out-of-distribution in-distribution. This is how generative AI works. This is how even self-driving cars work. Make sure that you cover all the roads, corner cases, everything. That should go into your training data.

This is really different from how humans learn to drive. We do not need to see a lot of these corner-case examples. We just deal with it, which is the real mystery of intelligence that I wish one day we will have some answers for. We're so data-efficient. But right now, generative AI—the only way, under this current framework and current paradigm, is making sure that all the out-of-distribution becomes in-distribution. However you do it, just make sure that's going to happen. That's why post-training requires curating a lot of data, or synthesizing and curating, and taking some combination of the two. Even that's not enough, therefore you do reinforcement learning at scale, because reinforcement learning is another way of making out-of-distribution in-distribution, by having the model explore itself all these other unexplored areas. Make sure that it's all explored before you get into the testing phase.

items.question: How do you use reinforcement learning during pre-training to encourage a language model to think for itself?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as a pre-training objective
items.answer: Roughly speaking, the idea is that during pre-training the model is forced to be completely passive in the way that it learns to predict which token comes next. But what if we encourage the model to think for itself before predicting the next token? What if we encourage the model to think for itself by generating something like a chain of thought and then predict the next token? In that context, the reward—because it's reinforcement learning, we now need to think about reward—the reward could be different things, but the key idea of our approach is to make the reward information gain of predicting the next token with thought compared to without thought. Now you have to be able to predict the next token even better than yourself predicting the next token without a thought. You have to learn to think better so that your next-token prediction probability becomes better than your own prediction probability without a thought. That way we encourage the model to think for itself before answering the next token.

items.question: How do you view debiasing as an approach to making AI serve people with different values and cultural norms?
items.object: Debiasing AI and respecting diverse cultural values
items.answer:
I don't think debiasing is the right answer, in the sense that debiasing is also impossible, but also that sometimes you do want to maintain your own bias. For example, if you're a religious person or if you're from a certain country where you have particular norms that you like to go by, then maybe we want to respect that.

As a human, when we interact with other human beings who we know have different values, we have a way of navigating around this person such that we maintain politeness, maintain respect, and agree to disagree, right? To some degree, I think this is very important: AI is aware of diverse values and then able to navigate around it, as opposed to just being completely neutral everywhere, which may not only be unattainable but also may not be the desirable solution if we are trying to really serve different cultural norms in a respectful manner.

items.question: How do you think an LLM should answer politically thorny questions that have multiple reasonable answers?
items.object: LLM responses to politically thorny questions
items.answer: I think the best way might be for an LLM to just present all of them—all of the reasonable opinions—as, "The answer is that people have different opinions. Here's one view, here's another view," and be able to include all of them as opposed to picking the majority opinion, because that marginalizes the rest.

items.question: How do you think distributional pluralism should guide AI systems that must make categorical decisions?
items.object: Distributional pluralism in AI decision-making
items.answer: Distributional pluralism is when AI is made for more like decision-making processes, where maybe AI is doing job application filtering or answering questions that it has to answer in a more categorical manner. You have to choose an answer; you cannot give all of the answers. Then distributionally, the distribution of LLM decisions should mimic the distribution of human decisions. At each point in time AI might be making a decision that differs from any other human decisions. However, when we look at the overall distribution, instead of going for the majority case all the time—which would be distributionally super-skewed—the idea is to try to be more, at least distributionally, even compared to now. Of course, humans have a bias, so it's not like our distribution of decisions is necessarily fair or unbiased, right? But at least let's not get worse than that.

items.question: What role do you see steerable pluralism playing in the everyday use of AI models?

items.answer: I think steerable pluralism is that you're able to steer the model to different values, your moral framework or value framework, to serve your day-to-day need within the scope that's reasonable to execute this. In some scenarios you might want to be more or less pluralistic in the way the model operates.

items.question: How do you assess the state of research on aligning AI models with diverse human values?
items.object: Research on pluralistic alignment of AI models
items.answer:
This sort of research requires both data research as well as algorithmic research. To my delight, a lot of smart academics started developing solutions for both fronts. There are some new algorithms that do more pluralistic alignment, for example, distributional pluralism. Other people are working on this.

One could argue that the frontier models are not so bad. Frontier models in general are better at this kind of pluralistic alignment compared to open-source models that went through less effort in terms of data curation and safety guardrails and everything. In the spirit of making smaller, especially open-source, models more powerful for wider accessibility, this requires more academic research to share data, make data and share data, as well as coming up with algorithmic innovations in order to get around the limitations of the data. It's still a lot of work to be done, but at least there's community effort.

items.question: Why are you personally excited about pursuing AI for science?
items.object: AI for science
items.answer: I'm quite excited about that personally because the positive impact of AI for scientific domains can be phenomenal. If we know how to do it quite right, medicine and different aspects of human life could really benefit from AI for science. That's also a really hard intellectual challenge because that really requires being able to reach knowledge that's really above and beyond human knowledge reflected on the internet data. The thing is, AI is only really good at learning the data that humans are able to provide. This is a big intellectual challenge as well, and I'm very excited about pursuing further in that direction.
